oneLiner.en: Before Shabbos Zachor and Purim the Mashgiach explains that reading Parshas Zachor weakens the inner force of Amalek, the yetzer hara, and that Purim is a day of hidden, exalted kedushah to be spent in seriousness, prayer and closeness to Hashem, not in drinking and smoking.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by explaining that everything has an inner life-force, and that Amalek's inner force is the yetzer hara that cools a Jew's emunah. Amalek cannot be fought with weapons, but reading Parshas Zachor weakens that force; it will be erased completely only with Moshiach. He asks the one reading and the listeners to have in mind to fulfill the mitzvah, links the war on Amalek to teshuvah and to coming properly to davening on Shabbos, and stresses Hodu at Minchah of Erev Shabbos. He then turns to Purim: the three days before it are like the days of preparation before Shavuos, Yom Kippur is only 'like Purim', and on Purim Hashem shows love to the lowest Jew and gives to whoever stretches out his hand. Purim's kedushah is so high that Hashem's name is hidden in the Megillah. He warns at length against getting drunk and smoking on Purim, and closes urging the bochurim to daven on time.

en: Amalek's inner force is the yetzer hara that cools emunah, and reading Parshas Zachor weakens that force even though Amalek cannot be fought physically.
Until Moshiach comes Amalek can only be weakened, as Yehoshua only weakened him; his full erasure belongs to the time of Moshiach.
The remedy for the Amalek within a person is teshuvah, and part of it is coming properly to davening on Shabbos and not talking or wandering during Hodu.
On Purim Hashem shows love to even the lowest Jew, and just as one gives to everyone who stretches out his hand, Hashem gives to whoever asks.
Purim's kedushah is higher even than Shabbos and Yom Kippur, so it is a day of serious joy with trembling, not of mockery and smoking.
Purim's kedushah comes from a level above the name Havayah, which is why Hashem's name appears in the Megillah only hidden in initial and final letters.
The Mashgiach says that, practically, it is better not to get drunk or smoke on Purim, since many become alcoholics and smokers precisely from Purim.

title.en: Amalek's inner force and Parshas Zachor

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that every creature has an inner life-force, and that Amalek's is the yetzer hara that cools emunah; he cites the Gerrer Rebbe's tradition that the Germans are Amalek. Since Amalek cannot be fought with weapons, reading Parshas Zachor weakens his force, though only Moshiach will erase him completely.

title.en: Hearing Zachor, teshuvah and Shabbos davening

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks the reader and listeners of Parshas Zachor to intend to fulfill the mitzvah and to pray for help against Amalek, names teshuvah as the answer to the Amalek that makes bochurim sin, and decries standing at the bulletin board during Hodu. He brings Rebbe Mottel Slonimer on talking during Hodu and a story of a Rebbe who put the Shabbos tisch and davening before saying all of Tehillim.

title.en: The days before Purim and its love

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Vorker Rebbe that the three days before Purim are like the three days of preparation before Shavuos, and that Yom Kippur is only 'like Purim'. On Purim Hashem annulled the decree and showed love to the lowest Jew, and the giving to all who stretch out a hand, a special mitzvah beyond ordinary tzedakah, mirrors how Hashem gives to whoever asks.

title.en: Kedushas keser and the open Megillah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the kedushah of keser shines on Purim all day, more than on Shabbos, so Purim is a serious day of joy with trembling and not of cigarettes and jokes. Great kedushah is usually covered, like the shofar, the challos, the matzos and the Sefer Torah, but on Purim the whole Megillah is spread open because its kedushah spreads over the world.

title.en: Hashem's hidden name in the Megillah

summary.en: The Mashgiach says, as something he himself does not fully understand, that Purim's kedushah comes from a level above the name Havayah, citing the Ba'al HaTanya on 'before Hashem you shall be purified'. Therefore Hashem's name is not openly in the Megillah, only in initial and final letters, and on Purim, as the King asked Esther, Hashem grants requests.

title.en: Not drinking and not smoking on Purim

summary.en: The Mashgiach warns the bochurim not to get drunk: the true talmidim of the Ba'al Shem Tov did not get drunk on Purim, there is a machlokes Rishonim, and practically it is better not to. He describes Jews he knows who became alcoholics and smokers from Purim, explains that the habit cannot be controlled, and suggests drinking a cup of wine and lying down to sleep.

title.en: Esther and the moon; davening on time

summary.en: The Mashgiach mentions that Esther is compared to the moon, as the Gemara says, with deep secrets in this, and recalls the Kaliver Rebbe's holy niggunim. He closes urging the bochurim to come on time to davening, especially on Shabbos Zachor and Purim, and to daven with fire.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains to bachurim the ten sefiros, showing how the ten makkos in Egypt revealed the ten utterances of creation and illustrating each middah with examples from life and from the Avos.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Mishnah that the world was created with ten utterances, which come in two sets, the mind and the middos. Since no one saw creation, Hashem showed its ten powers through the ten makkos, which is why the first of the Ten Commandments speaks of the Exodus. The makkos match the utterances in reverse: the plague of the firstborn matches Bereishis, the beginning, which the Gemara counts as an utterance although it has no 'vayomer'; darkness matches 'let there be light'. He then explains chochmah, binah and daas through a student working out a Gemara, and chesed and gevurah through love and restraint, with daas as the link between mind and middos. Tiferes is a beautiful blend, seen in Yaakov, whose children were all holy, unlike Avraham's pure chesed and Yitzchak's pure gevurah. Netzach and hod are the two legs, fighting or fleeing; yesod is continuity and malchus is bittul. The shiur ends with a seudah, l'chaim and a niggun.

en: The world was created with ten utterances, which divide into two sets: the mind (mochin) and the middos.
Since no one saw creation, Hashem displayed its ten powers through the ten makkos, which correspond to the ten utterances in reverse order.
Chochmah is the first flash of an idea, binah builds it into a full structure, and daas connects the mind to the middos.
Chesed and gevurah are opposite middos, and daas is knowing when to use each.
Tiferes is a beautiful blend of chesed and gevurah, which is why only holy children came from Yaakov.
Netzach and hod are the two legs a person stands on, two opposite ways to survive: winning the fight or yielding and fleeing.
Yesod is continuation through the generations, and malchus is bittul, accepting the yoke of Heaven.

title.en: Ten utterances shown through ten makkos

summary.en: The Mashgiach introduces the ten sefiros, explained in the Tanya, through the Mishnah that the world was created with ten utterances in two sets, mind and middos. He asks why the first commandment mentions the Exodus rather than creation, and answers that no one saw creation, while all of Israel saw the ten makkos, which revealed its ten powers.

title.en: The makkos match the utterances in reverse

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that the makkos correspond to the utterances backwards. Bereishis counts as the tenth utterance, the beginning before any speech existed, and matches the plague of the firstborn; 'let there be light' matches darkness, and the third utterance, the heavens, matches the locusts that came from the sky. He adds that the Bnei Yissaschar works out every pair.

title.en: Chochmah, binah, daas; chesed and gevurah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains chochmah as the first flash of an answer to a Gemara question, binah as building it into a full structure, and daas as connecting the mind to the middos. He defines chesed as love and giving and gevurah as restraint, and shows with the example of eating twenty cookies and of insulting a friend in anger what happens when a middah is used without daas.

title.en: Tiferes, the blend, and the Avos

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains tiferes as a blend, like many colors in a beautiful picture, and as a rebbe's love for a talmid mixed with fear. He links the seven middos to the seven ushpizin: Avraham's pure chesed produced Yishmael, Yitzchak's pure gevurah produced Esav, while Yaakov's tiferes produced only the twelve holy shevatim.

title.en: Netzach and hod, yesod and malchus

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Pesach Eliyahu, printed in the siddur, that the sefiros correspond to the limbs of the body, and explains netzach and hod as the two legs a person stands on. With a mashal of a dog on a country road he shows them as opposite ways to survive, overcoming or fleeing, and ties hod to bowing at Modim; he ends briefly with yesod as continuity and malchus as bittul.

title.en: Yahrzeit seudah, l'chaim and niggun

summary.en: The Mashgiach mentions that it is a yahrzeit that night and makes a seudah with l'chaim, blessing the bachurim with health and success in ruchniyus and gashmiyus. The shiur ends with the song chassidim sang when parting from their rebbe after Yom Tov.

oneLiner.en: At a lechaim, the Mashgiach says the nations constantly scheme against the small Jewish people, and brings the three pesukim the children told Mordechai, beginning with 'Al tira', as a source of emunah that their plans will not stand.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with a Rebbe of all of Poland whose disciples were all the great tzaddikim of Poland, among them Ger, Alexander and Vorka. He then says the Jews are a small people, the fewest of the nations, yet always make the headlines; the world constantly talks about them and everyone sets himself against them. The situation, he says, gets worse and worse, which in other words means better and better. Recalling a great war in which great miracles beyond nature were seen, he says one must rely only on the Ribono shel Olam. He retells the Midrash that when Haman sought to harm Mordechai, three children each told Mordechai a passuk, beginning with 'Al tira mipachad pisom' and 'Utzu eitzah'. With these pesukim, he says, one must strengthen oneself in emunah that the plans of the world's great ones against the Jews will not stand, and rejoice that a great time of salvation is coming.

en: The Jews are the smallest of the nations, yet the world constantly talks about them and sets itself against them.
The Mashgiach says the situation getting worse and worse means, in other words, that it is getting better and better.
One must rely only on the Ribono shel Olam, as in a great war when open miracles beyond nature were seen.
The pesukim the children told Mordechai teach that the plans of the nations against the Jews will not stand, for Hashem is with us.

title.en: Al tira: emunah against the nations' plans

summary.en: After mentioning a Rebbe whose disciples were the great tzaddikim of Poland, the Mashgiach speaks of the world's constant preoccupation with the Jews, retells the Midrash of the three children's pesukim to Mordechai, and urges strengthening emunah that the nations' plans will not stand.

catalogTitle: ברכת קריאת שמע Elevates us for Our Private Audience with Hashem (שמונה עשרה)

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach shows how Krias Shema and its brachos, above all the remembrance of Yetzias Mitzrayim in Emes V'yatziv, lift a person step by step until he stands before the King in Shemoneh Esrei.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach describes davening as an ascent through the four worlds, ending with Shemoneh Esrei, the climax of tefillah, where a Jew returns to the root of his soul, the Avos. He discusses kavanah in the first bracha and urges learning Sefer Bereishis to know the Avos. Krias Shema holds many mitzvos: accepting Hashem's kingship, readiness for mesiras nefesh, and finally remembering Yetzias Mitzrayim, the basis of emunah and the root of every later redemption. In Mitzrayim the Jews also suffered a spiritual exile, a closed heart that could not daven; the Exodus opened their hearts and mouths, so mentioning it at length before Shemoneh Esrei opens ours. In Shemoneh Esrei one stands in thought in the Kodesh HaKodashim, climbing fifteen steps through the fifteen words of Emes V'yatziv, whose eight 'emes' should not be rushed. Finally one stands before Hashem like David HaMelech, as a poor man.

en: Davening ascends through the four worlds, and Shemoneh Esrei is its climax, where one stands before the King and returns to the root of the soul.
Krias Shema contains many mitzvos, including readiness for mesiras nefesh, and is completed only with the remembrance of Yetzias Mitzrayim.
Yetzias Mitzrayim, witnessed by the whole nation, is the basis of emunah and contains the power of every later redemption.
The Exodus freed the Jews from a spiritual exile in which their hearts were closed and they could not daven, so mentioning it before Shemoneh Esrei opens the heart and mouth.
In Shemoneh Esrei a person stands in thought in the Kodesh HaKodashim, and the fifteen words of Emes V'yatziv are fifteen steps up to it.
The eight times 'emes' in Emes V'yatziv should be said slowly and internalized, not rushed.
One should enter Shemoneh Esrei like David HaMelech, as a poor man who has nothing, because the tefillah of the poor man is the strongest.

title.en: Ascending the four worlds to Shemoneh Esrei

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that creation came down through four worlds, Atzilus, Beriah, Yetzirah and Asiyah, and that davening climbs back up through them to Shemoneh Esrei, the climax of tefillah. Tefillah is the mitzvah of serving Hashem with the heart, and in it a Jew returns to the root of his soul, Avraham Avinu.

title.en: Kavanah in Avos and knowing the Avos

summary.en: The Mashgiach discusses the requirement of kavanah in the first bracha, why today one does not repeat Shemoneh Esrei without it, and the difference between fulfilling the rabbinic and the Torah mitzvah of tefillah. In a parenthetical remark he urges learning Sefer Bereishis well, since one cannot have kavanah in Avos without knowing the Avos.

title.en: The mitzvos of Krias Shema

summary.en: The Mashgiach lists the mitzvos contained in Krias Shema: readiness for mesiras nefesh, which atones like dying al kiddush Hashem, accepting Hashem's kingship and His oneness, love of Hashem, and finally remembering Yetzias Mitzrayim. He explains that emunah rests on the Exodus that the whole nation witnessed, and that it holds the redemptions of every generation and individual.

title.en: Remembering and elaborating on the Exodus

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the passuk that answers the fear of the nations with 'remember what Hashem did to Pharaoh', and explains that remembering the Exodus is itself a protection. He cites the rule that one who does not say Emes V'yatziv has not fulfilled his obligation, and explains that Emes V'yatziv is where one elaborates on the Exodus and the splitting of the sea.

title.en: The double exile and the opened heart

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that in Mitzrayim the Jews were in a physical and a spiritual exile: their hearts were closed and they could not daven or feel close to Hashem, like the blockage one sometimes feels in davening. The Exodus opened the gates of tefillah, which is why it is called Pesach, the mouth that speaks, and mentioning it before Shemoneh Esrei opens our hearts and mouths.

title.en: Standing in the Kodesh HaKodashim

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that in Shemoneh Esrei one should imagine standing in the Beis HaMikdash in the Kodesh HaKodashim, because a person is where his thought is, and he proves this from the halacha of one who sets his Shabbos place by a tree. The fifteen steps up to the Azarah correspond to the fifteen Shir HaMaalos and to fifteen words beginning with vav in Emes V'yatziv.

title.en: Not rushing Emes V'yatziv: the eight 'emes'

summary.en: The Mashgiach laments the habit of rushing Emes V'yatziv and tells of a tzaddik who protested a chazzan's speed with a mashal of meat pulled from a hungry man's mouth. He explains the four times 'emes' after Yetzias Mitzrayim as corresponding to the four exiles, Bavel, Paras, Yavan and Edom, and another four that reinforce them, eight in all, which one should say slowly and absorb.

title.en: Approaching the King as a poor man

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes how David HaMelech, who had everything, saw himself as a poor man with nothing, and how such a request is granted. He brings three kinds of tefillah, of Moshe (contemplation of Hashem's greatness), of David (song and joy) and of the poor man (a broken heart), the last being the strongest, and concludes that before Shemoneh Esrei we take on David HaMelech's stance as poor men.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach asks the bochurim to strengthen the tefillah of the beis medrash in a time that calls for crying out to Hashem, and to thank Hashem every day for the privilege of being in Eretz Yisrael.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach recalls that the beis medrash was founded on tefillah: bochurim who had davened with set seder in camp felt it missing when they returned to yeshiva and asked to continue in a shtibel. He brings the Ba'al HaTanya, citing the Arizal, that in the generation before Moshiach the main avodah is tefillah, and stresses that tefillah does not contradict Torah; one who davens with some closeness to Hashem learns differently all day. People take tefillah lightly, as the Gemara says of things that stand at the height of the world. Just as the Jews left Mitzrayim by crying out to Hashem, today, with a hard situation in Eretz Yisrael and the world, one must cry out for mercy, so he asks them to come and daven together. He then asks them to set aside a couple of minutes daily to thank Hashem for being in Eretz Yisrael, tells how Jews used to spitting on the ground had to learn to respect its holy earth, and ends with Torah, tefillah, chesed and unity.

en: The beis medrash was founded on tefillah, at the request of bochurim who missed the davening they had in camp.
In the generation before Moshiach the main avodah is tefillah, and tefillah does not contradict Torah but changes how one learns all day.
As the Jews left Mitzrayim by crying out to Hashem, so today, in a hard situation, one must cry out for mercy.
The Mashgiach asks the bochurim to set aside a couple of minutes each day to thank Hashem for the privilege of being in Eretz Yisrael.
Being chosen to be in Eretz Yisrael when many Jews are not makes a greater obligation, to be filled through Torah, tefillah and chesed.

candidateTopics: tefillah in the generation before Moshiach

title.en: Strengthening the tefillah of the beis medrash

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how the beis medrash was founded on tefillah, brings the Ba'al HaTanya that tefillah is the avodah before Moshiach, and compares today's need to cry out to the crying out in Mitzrayim. He asks the bochurim to come and daven together, weekdays and Shabbos.

title.en: Thanking Hashem for Eretz Yisrael

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks for a couple of minutes a day of thanks for being in Eretz Yisrael, tells of Jews from Europe who had to learn not to spit on its holy ground, and calls for Torah, tefillah, chesed and unity. He closes with a brachah to meet again in Yerushalayim, followed by singing.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the whole month of Nisan is a month of emunah, shows through the gematria of the Name Havayah how matzah carries holy Names that bring emunah into a Jew, and calls on each bachur to renew himself on Pesach as all of creation is renewed.

abstract.en: Speaking at Shabbos Hachodesh, the Mashgiach describes Nisan as a month in which the whole month is Yom Tov, a month that strengthens emunah, climaxing at the Seder, when one tells the children of yetzias Mitzrayim, the foundation of emunah. The ten plagues, matching the ten utterances of creation in reverse, testify that Hashem created the world. Everything has a soul of holy letters and Names; bread equals three times the Name Havayah, while matzah equals three times the Name with its milui. Hence 'ha lachma anya': the Names in our matzah are those eaten in Egypt. Matzah is the os of chol hamoed, so the Mashgiach urges mehudar matzah at least at the Seder. He closes with Nisan as the season of renewal for the world and every Jew.

en: In Nisan the whole month, not only the day of Yom Tov, is holy, and the month is a time to strengthen emunah.
Yetzias Mitzrayim is the foundation of emunah, and the ten plagues testify that Hashem created the world with ten utterances.
Every thing in the world has a body and a soul, and its soul is the holy letters and Names through which it was created.
Bread equals three times the Name Havayah, while matzah equals three times the Name with its milui, so matzah is a far higher food.
Matzah is the os of a Jew on chol hamoed, so the Mashgiach urges eating matzah baked with kedushah, at least at the Seder.
Pesach is the time when the Jewish people and all of creation are renewed, and each Jew must renew himself too.

title.en: Nisan, a month of emunah

summary.en: On Shabbos Hachodesh the Mashgiach explains that in Nisan the whole month is Yom Tov and a time to strengthen emunah. Its climax is the Seder night, when one lowers oneself to tell the children of yetzias Mitzrayim, on which the mitzvah of emunah in Anochi rests.

title.en: The ten plagues and the ten utterances

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks how we know the world was created, since no one was there, and answers that the ten plagues testify to it: counted from the end they match the ten utterances of creation, from makkas bechoros against 'Bereishis' to darkness against 'let there be light'. Each plague broke the klipah of heresy and brought emunah into the Jews.

title.en: The holy Names inside bread

summary.en: From 'not by bread alone does man live' the Mashgiach explains that everything has a body and a soul, the holy letters that form it, as with 'shor' and 'even'. A Jew who washes and says the ten-word hamotzi and dips three times in salt takes in the Name Havayah three times, which is the gematria of lechem.

title.en: Lechem and matzah in gematria

summary.en: The Mashgiach works out with the bachurim that the Name Havayah with its milui equals 45, the gematria of adam, and three times 45 is 135, the gematria of matzah. Matzah is therefore a far higher bread than lechem, and this is the 'motza pi Hashem' by which man lives.

title.en: Ha lachma anya: the same Names

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the question on 'ha lachma anya', how one can call our matzah the bread eaten in Egypt, and answers that the holy Names inside it are the same; the matzah is only an envelope. He then speaks of the levels of matzah, up to chaburah matzah baked by ehrliche yungeleit.

title.en: Matzah as the os of chol hamoed

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts matzah baked without kedushah with chaburah matzah, then explains that a Jew needs two osos, bris milah and tefillin; on Shabbos and, according to the Mechaber, on chol hamoed the day itself and the matzah take the place of tefillin. Since matzah is the os, he urges eating mehudar matzah at least at the Seder.

title.en: Pesach, the season of renewal

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that at yetzias Mitzrayim the family of Yaakov became a new nation, and every Pesach the Jewish people and each Jew are renewed; this is seen below in the trees, fields and birds of Nisan and in new clothes and dishes. He calls on each bachur to become a new person in learning, davening and middos.

title.en: Brachos for Pesach, lechaim and singing

summary.en: The Mashgiach blesses the bachurim with a kosher and joyous Pesach and with eating matzos in Yerushalayim with the korban Pesach; the gathering ends with lechaim and a niggun.

oneLiner.en: Speaking to yeshiva bochurim before Rosh Hashanah, the Mashgiach shows from the number of pesukim in the parshiyos of the season that there are 122 days of teshuvah from Rosh Chodesh Elul until Zos Chanukah, warns not to waste them as in the past year, and calls on bnei Torah to learn with truth and refinement for all of Klal Yisrael.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach tells the bochurim he will speak words of remez. The forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Yom Kippur are the formation of the year, like the forty days in which the Gemara says a fetus is formed, and the Ba'al HaTurim explains zachar as brachah. He then lists the windows of judgment: thirty days for complete tzaddikim, forty for beinonim, fifty-two until Shmini Atzeres per the Zohar, and 122 until Zos Chanukah per the Arizal. Since the number of pesukim in a sedra may be darshened, as the Midrash shows with the seventy days of Haman's decree, he finds these numbers in Nitzavim, Vayeilech and Haazinu. A listener noted that Ki Savo also has 122 pesukim; the Mashgiach explains it points back at last year's 122 days, which the year's calamities show were not used. He urges bnei Torah to carry Klal Yisrael, to learn Torah with preparation, truth and refinement, and blesses them.

en: The forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Yom Kippur are the forty days in which the coming year is formed, like the formation of a fetus.
There are several windows of teshuvah: thirty days for complete tzaddikim, forty for beinonim, fifty-two until Shmini Atzeres, and 122 until the last day of Chanukah.
The number of pesukim in each sedra is part of the Torah and may be darshened.
Nitzavim has forty pesukim, and together with Vayeilech and Haazinu the count reaches 122, matching the days of teshuvah.
Ki Savo's 122 pesukim point back at last year's 122 days, which the year's calamities show were not used properly.
Bnei Torah carry the responsibility for all of Klal Yisrael, and Torah learning with truth and refinement is what protects from the birthpangs of Moshiach.

title.en: The forty days that form the year

summary.en: The Mashgiach thanks the Rosh Yeshiva and says he will speak words of remez. He compares the forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Yom Kippur to the forty days in which a fetus is formed, and brings the Ba'al HaTurim that zachar is gematria brachah.

title.en: Thirty, forty, fifty-two and 122 days

summary.en: From the Gemara, the Zohar and the Arizal the Mashgiach lists the stages of judgment: Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur, Hoshana Rabbah and Shmini Atzeres, and Zos Chanukah. He counts the days from Rosh Chodesh Elul, using the Gemara's rule that a plain month is thirty days, and arrives at 122.

title.en: Counting pesukim: Haman's seventy days

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Masorah's count of pesukim in each sedra may be darshened. As an example he brings the Midrash that the seventy days from Haman's decree on Pesach until the new letters in Sivan were a reward to the nations for mourning Yaakov Avinu seventy days, and that the Megillah has seventy pesukim from the decree to its annulment.

title.en: Nitzavim, Vayeilech, Haazinu: 122 pesukim

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that the parshiyos read in the season of teshuvah match the windows of days: Nitzavim has forty pesukim, and through Vayeilech and Haazinu they reach 122. He then reports that a listener in America pointed out that Ki Savo also has 122 pesukim, and asks why the hint is doubled.

title.en: What the past year's events demand

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks whether last year's tefillos succeeded, and points to the year's calamities, the earthquake and the storm in New York, as messengers of Hashem. He retells the Chafetz Chaim's derashah about the Mississippi flood, and lists the murder of a child, the passing of three gedolei Yisrael in three weeks, and other tragedies as signs that Hashem demands something.

title.en: Ki Savo as a pointing finger

summary.en: The Mashgiach answers the double hint: Ki Savo, read so that the past year end with its curses, reminds that last year there were 122 days and asks whether they were used in Torah, tefillah and middos; Nitzavim through Haazinu give the new 122 days. He urges not to repeat the mistake.

title.en: Bnei Torah carry Klal Yisrael

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells the bochurim that the year's destiny rests on them, as bnei Torah born into homes of Torah, to do teshuvah and take resolutions for all of Klal Yisrael. He describes the need for rachamim in Eretz Yisrael, the miracles seen there, the growth of Torah, and the state of the world that calls for geulah amid the birthpangs of Moshiach.

title.en: Learning Torah with truth and refinement

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that Torah and gemilus chasadim save from the birthpangs of Moshiach, and describes how to learn: a moment of preparation before sitting down, the Maharal that the place of learning halacha is today's Beis HaMikdash, admitting the truth to a chavrusa, and refinement. He closes with the Chasam Sofer's acronym of ish and a brachah for a year of geulah.

catalogTitle: The Accomplishments of תפילה are Different each Day

oneLiner.en: Starting from facing the Beis HaMikdash in tefillah, the Mashgiach teaches that a person is where his thoughts are, and that a Yid should seek to give Hashem nachas ruach beyond what he is commanded, with tevilas Ezra, mikvah and Rabbeinu Tam tefillin as examples.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Shlomo's tefillah that prayers in exile be directed toward the Beis HaMikdash, explains how to face Eretz Yisrael from Borough Park, and says one should have in mind standing in the Kodesh HaKodashim. He brings the Ba'al Shem Tov that a person is where his thought is, and the Satmar Rav's proof from the techum Shabbos case of a traveler who fixes his eyes on a tree. Turning to Ezra's takanah of tevilah before learning and davening, he brings his rebbe Reb Shraga Feivel and the Mesilas Yesharim: a loving servant or child does what pleases his master even unasked. He contrasts Bilam with Avraham at the Akeidah, then shows Hashem desires taharah: the Rambam's letter, the Kohen Gadol's tevilos, mikvah before Shabbos. A story of Reb Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld, Rabbeinu Tam tefillin and the shofar sounds illustrate the theme, ending with the Rambam on bodily purity bringing purity of soul.

en: When davening, a person should face toward Eretz Yisrael and have in mind that he is standing in the Beis HaMikdash, before the Kodesh HaKodashim.
Following the Ba'al Shem Tov, a person is located where his thought is, so thoughts of Torah place him in Gan Eden and forbidden thoughts in Gehinnom.
A loving servant or child does not only what he is told but what he knows will please his master or parent; so should a Yid act toward Hashem.
Although Ezra's takanah of tevilah became void, Hashem's desire for avodah in taharah remains, making mikvah a midas chassidus.
Customs such as Rabbeinu Tam tefillin are not an obligation but an extra nachas ruach for Hashem.

title.en: The Satmar Rav's proof from techum Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Satmar Rav's support for the Ba'al Shem Tov from the din of a traveler far from the city at nightfall who fixes his eyes on a tree and makes it his place. He concludes that one must guard his thoughts, and that one who fixes his mind on the Beis HaMikdash is truly there.

title.en: Ezra's takanah and doing Hashem's will

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes Ezra's takanah requiring tevilah after keri before learning and davening, which did not take hold and became void. He then brings his rebbe Reb Shraga Feivel and the Mesilas Yesharim: a servant or child who loves does what pleases his master unasked, and contrasts Bilam, who tried again and again to bend Hashem's will to his own.

title.en: Avraham at the Akeidah

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes how Avraham, despite Hashem's promise that the Jewish nation would come from Yitzchak, did not argue or daven to change the decree but went to the Akeidah with simcha, keeping pace with Yitzchak as Rashi explains. He returns to the Mesilas Yesharim's image of the devoted son.

title.en: Hashem desires avodah in taharah

summary.en: Reb Shraga Feivel applied this to tevilas Ezra: the requirement of taharah in the Mikdash shows Hashem favors avodah in purity, so though the takanah is void, mikvah is a midas chassidus. The Mashgiach brings the Rambam's letter that he himself kept it though he could not rule it as halachah, the Kohen Gadol's tevilos on Yom Kippur, and mikvah before Shabbos and on Shabbos morning per the Arizal.

title.en: Reb Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld and the mikvah

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how Reb Isser Zalman Meltzer saw Reb Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld leaving the mikvah and asked about the lost learning time; he answered that if a mikvah can make a ger into a Yid, it can make a Yid into a better Yid. The Mashgiach stresses he is not ruling that one must go daily, only that a Yid should seek to give Hashem nachas ruach, like a child bringing his mother a gift.

title.en: Rabbeinu Tam tefillin and the shofar

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the custom of wearing Rabbeinu Tam tefillin after marriage: the dispute goes back to two ancient practices, the halachah follows Rashi, but the Zohar says both are needed, and starting after the chasunah follows the Gemara's view that one can then learn in purity. He compares the shofar sounds, where the Zohar says both shevarim and teruos are needed, and closes with the Rambam that purity of body brings purity of soul.

oneLiner.en: Before Rosh Chodesh Nissan the Mashgiach tells the bachurim that just as the whole world renews itself in Nissan, a Jew must renew himself, chiefly by strengthening his emunah through eating matzah with kavanah and through real, unhurried davening.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens on Shabbos Mevorchim Nissan: Nissan is the head of the months, a time when Hashem's chesed pours onto the world and everything renews itself, from the trees to the Jewish custom of new clothes for Pesach. A Jew must renew himself too, by taking on the yoke of Heaven in Torah, tefillah, middos and chesed, and by making whole vessels to receive the blessing. Pesach is the yom tov of emunah, tied to Avraham Avinu, and matzah is an 'emunah vitamin', so it should be guarded carefully and eaten with kavanah all of Pesach. Emunah is strengthened mainly through tefillah: the Mashgiach urges the bachurim to use the minyan of their beis medrash, to say Hodu, Shiras HaYam and Emes V'Yatziv with life, and tells of the Lubliner's notebook on the first twelve days of Nissan. He closes with Pesach as the 'mouth that speaks' and the rare Birkas HaChamah on Erev Pesach.

en: Nissan is the head of the months; Hashem's chesed pours onto the world and the whole creation renews itself, so a Jew must renew himself as well.
A Jew renews himself by accepting the yoke of Heaven in Torah, tefillah, middos and chesed, and he needs whole vessels to receive the blessings.
Pesach is the yom tov of emunah, corresponding to Avraham Avinu, and matzah is an 'emunah vitamin' to be guarded carefully and eaten with kavanah.
Emunah is strengthened above all through tefillah, since praying itself is an act of believing that Hashem can provide.
Each of the first twelve days of Nissan governs a month of the year, so how one davens and behaves on those days matters greatly.
Weekday davening, especially Shiras HaYam and Emes V'Yatziv, should be said with warmth and without rushing, since they bring a person into emunah.

title.en: Nissan, the month of renewal

title.en: How a Jew renews himself; Pesach and emunah

summary.en: The Mashgiach says a Jew renews himself by accepting the yoke of Heaven in Torah, tefillah, middos and chesed, and brings the Gemara about havdalah and sons to show that blessings need whole vessels. He then explains that Pesach is the yom tov of emunah, corresponding to Avraham Avinu, at whose home matzos were baked for the angels.

title.en: Matzah, the vitamin of emunah

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares matzah to a vitamin that puts emunah into a person, which is why one is careful with the quality and kashrus of matzos and with any concern of chametz. He urges eating matzah with kavanah, especially at the Seder, and explains that eating matzah the rest of Pesach is also a mitzvah, like eating in the sukkah.

title.en: Tefillah strengthens emunah

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells the bachurim that the chief strengthening of emunah is tefillah, and that their beis medrash holds a treasure: a minyan where one can prepare and daven properly instead of rushing. He describes how one who rushes Hodu rushes the whole davening, and explains that davening is itself emunah.

title.en: A child's kvitel and pure emunah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that even a simple person praying for his own needs is showing emunah, and tells of a kvitel he once read from a young boy asking for something childish, which showed real emunah because he turned to Hashem. He concludes that one should pour out the heart in davening and say Hodu with life.

title.en: The Lubliner's notebook of Nissan

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings from the Bnei Yissaschar that the Lubliner would write down on each of the first twelve days of Nissan what would happen in the corresponding month, and at year's end showed his talmidim that all had come true. He explains the Lubliner wished to show how each day of Nissan governs a whole month, so davening well on those days brings success.

title.en: Weekday davening, Shiras HaYam, Emes V'Yatziv

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts machine-like 'factory' davening with a warm, hand-made tefillah, and notes that many daven well on Shabbos but few on weekdays. He dwells on Shiras HaYam, which brings one into emunah, and on Emes V'Yatziv, bringing the Gemara that one who does not say it has not fulfilled his obligation and a gadol's complaint that people rush it.

title.en: Pesach, the speaking mouth; Birkas HaChamah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains Pesach as the mouth that speaks, coming out of its exile, and says the whole month of Nissan is Yetzias Mitzrayim, an opportunity to be used. After l'chaim and brachos for a kosher and joyous Pesach, he notes the rare Birkas HaChamah on Erev Pesach this year.

oneLiner.en: Opening with a story of the Rebbe Reb Elimelech in which the forces of impurity tremble at the Elul shofar, the Mashgiach explains that the frightening events of the time are Hashem's shofar, to be heard without fear, and calls on the people of Beitar to guard their place of tefillah and to strengthen ahavas Yisroel.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach tells a story of the Rebbe Reb Elimelech of Lizhensk: a man captured by the chitzonim (forces of impurity) is freed through the Rebbe's letter, and he remembers only that when Elul came and the shofar was blown, they all became frightened. The Mashgiach applies this to the present: in a time of great hester panim (Divine concealment), Hashem blows His shofar in another way, through floods, killings, the passing of three gedolim in one month and threats in the news. One must hear it and make a cheshbon, but not be afraid; he recalls how the Pnei Menachem and the Steipler kept learning during the sirens of the Gulf War. He then praises the davening in the beis medrash in Beitar, urges the people to guard and strengthen it against the Satan, to avoid disputes and to say the Rebbe Reb Elimelech's tefillah, seeing only their friends' virtues. He closes with Rachel's kosher jealousy, the need to build both Torah and tefillah, ahavas Yisroel, and brachos for the new year.

en: In the Rebbe Reb Elimelech's story the chitzonim became frightened when Elul came and the shofar was blown.
The Mashgiach says the events of the time, in a period of great hester panim, are Hashem's shofar blown in another way.
According to the Mashgiach one must hear the shofar and make a cheshbon, but one need not be afraid.
The Mashgiach calls the beis medrash in Beitar a place of tefillah that must be guarded and strengthened, because the Satan dislikes it.
He urges unity and avoiding disputes, even for the sake of Heaven, and seeing only the virtues of one's friend, as the Rebbe Reb Elimelech writes in his tefillah.

summary.en: The Mashgiach lists the frightening events in the world, in Eretz Yisroel and in America, and says this is Hashem's shofar for us, which must be heard without fear. He recalls the miracles after the war, the Torah's return to Eretz Yisroel, and the Pnei Menachem and Steipler learning on during the sirens, and concludes that each person must make a cheshbon in Elul.

title.en: Guarding the place of tefillah in Beitar

summary.en: The Mashgiach praises the beis medrash in Beitar, where visitors from America come to daven, and says he enjoyed the strong davening there. He urges the people to guard and strengthen it against the Satan, to be united without disputes, to say the Rebbe Reb Elimelech's tefillah, and he says the signs of Moshiach are visible in the news.

title.en: Kosher jealousy, Torah and tefillah, brachos

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains Rachel's jealousy of her sister as a kosher jealousy that begrudges nothing, brings the Gemara's dispute whether the place of Torah or of tefillah is greater and says both must be built up, cites Rabbi Akiva on loving one's fellow, and ends with brachos for a year of geulah, followed by singing.

catalogTitle: Why is it So Difficult to Daven in these Pre-Mashiach Times?

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that in the last days before Moshiach the Satan fights with new weapons against Hashem and Moshiach, and that tefillah, which is always an act of emunah, is what carries Klal Yisroel through.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Chofetz Chaim's statement that we live in ikvesa d'Meshicha, and argues with a coin analogy that every day there is a real chance Moshiach comes, despite all the years of waiting. He distinguishes the fixed ketz, known only to Hashem, from earlier moments when Moshiach could come, and recounts dates predicted by tzaddikim that turned into catastrophes, explaining that at such moments the Satan comes as accuser. The Gemara recorded a passed date to teach that disappointment must not shake emunah; Achashverosh and Daniel miscalculated, and even Rabbi Akiva was wrong about Bar Kochba. He then describes the signs of the footsteps of Moshiach: chutzpah, wrongdoing made lawful, inventions that destroy families, all weapons of the Satan fighting for his life. Against this, tefillah, though mocked, is always lishmah, since turning to Hashem is pure emunah, and emunah will bring the geulah.

en: Every day there is a real chance that Moshiach will come, no matter how long the wait has been.
Only Hashem knows the fixed time of Moshiach; dates predicted by tzaddikim passed and even turned into catastrophes.
A disappointment over a predicted date must not affect one's emunah; this is why the Gemara recorded a date that had already passed.
The signs of the generation before Moshiach are evident today: chutzpah, wrongdoing made lawful, and the breakdown of the family.
The Satan, fighting for his life before Moshiach, brings new inventions as weapons against Hashem and Moshiach.
Tefillah is mocked more than Torah, yet every tefillah is an exercise in emunah, and emunah is what will bring the geulah.

title.en: Moshiach could come any day

He adds that the fixed time of the geulah is known only to Hashem.

title.en: Predicted dates that became catastrophes

summary.en: The Mashgiach distinguishes the fixed ketz from times when Moshiach could be hastened, as in Mitzrayim, and lists dates tzaddikim gave: the Toldos Yaakov Yosef's Tav Shin, the year Tach, the Malbim's 1914, each of which brought catastrophe. He explains that at such a moment the Satan comes as accuser and brings up Klal Yisroel's sins.

title.en: Why the Gemara recorded a date that passed

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Ravina and Rav Ashi wrote a date for Moshiach that had already passed, and answers that it teaches not to let disappointment affect emunah. He then brings the Gemara in Megillah that Achashverosh, and even Daniel, miscalculated the seventy years.

title.en: Bar Kochba and the signs of Moshiach

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the Rambam, who writes halachos, tells the story of Ben Koziva whom Rabbi Akiva endorsed, and answers that it is itself a lesson: even Rabbi Akiva can be wrong about Moshiach. He then turns to the Gemara's signs of the footsteps of Moshiach, chutzpah and wrongdoing that has become lawful.

title.en: New inventions as the Satan's weapons

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts thousands of years of plow and sword with today's explosion of inventions, and explains that worse than weapons that could destroy the world are weapons against Hashem and Moshiach, as in the passuk about tearing off the bonds. The Satan, fighting for his life, uses them to destroy families and shalom bayis.

title.en: The backbone that carries Torah to Moshiach

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the promise that Torah will not be forgotten and Rabbi Yaakov Emden's words that Jewish survival in golus is a greater miracle than the splitting of the sea. A small backbone of Jews who keep Torah will carry over to the days of Moshiach, and he says they must thank Hashem and put in extra effort now.

title.en: Tefillah is mocked, yet it builds emunah

summary.en: The Mashgiach says tefillah especially is derided today, citing the Gemara that people scorn things that stand at the height of the world, while even one who does not learn still respects Torah. He explains that tefillah fosters emunah, and contrasts Torah learned shelo lishmah, which is justified only because it leads to lishmah.

title.en: A kvitel for a bicycle and a dog

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a kvitel at the Kosel in which a boy asked Hashem for a bicycle and a dog, and explains that the very act of turning to Hashem is lishmah and pure emunah, so every tefillah fortifies emunah. He closes with the Gemara that Chabakuk based everything on emunah, and that just as emunah preceded the song at the sea, emunah will bring the song of the geulah.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach tells the bochurim in Eretz Yisrael to value the privilege of being there, to use the opportunity to daven warmly together, to love their chavurah and guard their speech, and to do their part through Torah, tefillah and chesed.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the great privilege of being in Eretz Yisrael: every act there, learning Torah, washing negel vasser, even greeting a Jew, is many times greater and holier than abroad, so one must always thank Hashem. He tells how Jews from Poland, used to spitting, struggled with the habit in Eretz Yisrael, since one cannot spit on its earth. He recalls how the beis medrash grew out of loud, warm davening he introduced in camp about fifty years earlier, which the bochurim missed in yeshiva. He urges them to value the rare chance to daven at Emunas Yisrael, to come early on Shabbos and add each his spark to the flame, and to love their chavurah as the Ba'al Shem Tov's talmidim taught. He warns against speaking badly of any Jew, notes the worsening situation and the miracles in Eretz Yisrael since the war, and asks them to learn, daven and act well.

en: Every act a Jew does in Eretz Yisrael, even a simple one, is many times greater and holier than abroad, so one must constantly thank Hashem for being there.
The beis medrash grew out of warm, loud davening the Mashgiach introduced in camp, which the bochurim missed when they returned to yeshiva.
The bochurim should use the rare opportunity to daven at Emunas Yisrael, especially coming early on Shabbos, each adding his spark to the flame.
One must love every Jew, but one's own chavurah even more, and must not speak badly of any Jew.
Though the situation is worsening, the Mashgiach sees preparation for miracles, and asks each to do his part by learning, davening and being good.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains the forty-nine days of Sefirah as a climb out of forty-nine levels of impurity that Klal Yisrael also travels through in galus, and shows from the end of Maseches Sotah that the present world of chutzpah, high prices and heresy is ikvesa d'meshicha, the footsteps of Moshiach.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the gift of the Exodus: on the first night of Pesach the Jews were lifted out of the forty-nine gates of impurity, but from the second day they had to work their own way out, refining their middos over forty-nine days until Matan Torah. Citing the Ba'al Shem Tov, he says Klal Yisrael passes the same forty-nine stages in the desert journeys and in the long galus. He shows the pattern of 42 plus 7 in the journeys, in the 42-letter Name and Ana B'koach, and in Lamnatzeach. He then explains the custom of learning a daf of Maseches Sotah each day of Sefirah: the Omer of barley is like the sotah's offering, and Shavuos brings bread of wheat. The last daf describes ikvesa d'meshicha, and the Mashgiach shows its signs today: chutzpah, rising prices, a world that believes in nothing, and the suffering in Eretz Yisrael. He ends that one can rely only on our Father in Heaven.

en: The Exodus lifted the Jews out of the forty-nine gates of impurity as a gift; from the second day of Pesach they had to leave them by their own work, one level each day of Sefirah.
Citing the Ba'al Shem Tov, the Mashgiach teaches that Klal Yisrael passes the same forty-nine stages in the desert journeys and in the galus until the redemption.
Forty-two plus seven makes forty-nine: in the journeys, in the 42-letter Name said through Ana B'koach in the Sefirah count, and in Lamnatzeach.
Maseches Sotah, learned a daf a day during Sefirah, is tied to Sefirah: the Omer of barley tests the Jews like a sotah, and on Shavuos they bring wheat, human food.
The last daf of Sotah describes ikvesa d'meshicha, and the Mashgiach shows its signs in today's world: chutzpah, rising prices and a government turned to heresy.
The Mashgiach says a person who believes in nothing is more dangerous than an idolater, since faith, even false faith, held the nations back.

title.en: From the gift of the Exodus to the work of Sefirah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that on the first night of Pesach Hashem lifted the Jews out of the forty-nine gates of impurity as a gift, and from the second day they had to leave them by their own work. Counting forty-nine days, they refine the seven middos, seven times seven, to reach Matan Torah on the fiftieth.

title.en: Forty-nine journeys in the desert and in galus

summary.en: Citing the Ba'al Shem Tov, the Mashgiach says Klal Yisrael passes the same forty-nine stages: in the desert, a place of snakes and kelipos, and in the long galus, each era one journey. Parshas Masei lists forty-two journeys, and Rashi brings that they went back seven, making forty-nine.

title.en: The 42-letter Name, Ana B'koach and Lamnatzeach

summary.en: The Mashgiach connects the forty-nine journeys to the 42-letter Name, which Rabbi Nechunya ben Hakanah turned into the tefilah Ana B'koach. In the siddur each day of the count carries one letter, and at the end of each week the whole line is repeated, so forty-two becomes forty-nine; the same holds for the forty-nine words of Lamnatzeach.

title.en: A daf of Sotah each day: the sotah and the Omer

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the custom of learning one of the forty-nine dafim of Sotah each day of Sefirah, which helps one remember the count. The deeper reason: the Jews leaving Egypt were tested like a sotah, so the Omer was of barley, animal food, like the sotah's offering, and on Shavuos they bring the two loaves of wheat, human food, hinted in the milui of Hashem's Name beside the brachah.

title.en: The last daf of Sotah: ikvesa d'meshicha and chutzpah

summary.en: Each daf brings a person closer to Har Sinai; the last day of the count, malchus shebemalchus, matches the lowest level of galus, and the last daf of Sotah speaks of ikvesa d'meshicha. The Mashgiach notes that the Chafetz Chaim and other gedolim said it had already begun, and illustrates the foretold chutzpah with how respect for a teacher or a Rav has fallen.

title.en: Rising prices and a kingdom turned to heresy

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the law of supply and demand and says that before Moshiach prices rise against it, as the Baraisa foretells that wine will be dear though the vine gives fruit. He then explains that the kingdom turning to minus means believing in nothing, worse than idolatry, and tells how the Ba'al Shem Tov jumped off a wagon whose gentile driver did not cross himself before a priest.

title.en: From a world that believed to a world of minus

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts the past, when kings forced their subjects to believe and Jews gave their lives rather than convert, with America, founded on belief in G-d, and with today's world that believes in nothing, which the Gemara says is worse than a house of idolatry. He brings the Baraisa about the meeting house becoming a place of immorality, and describes a Williamsburg public school built with separate entrances for boys and girls.

title.en: The Galil, the poverty of Eretz Yisrael, and our Father in Heaven

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows the Baraisa's words on the Galil and on people wandering unpitied fulfilled in the rockets on the north and in fathers collecting for weddings, and says the whole Baraisa is fulfilled. He ends with the Gemara's last words, that one can rely only on our Father in Heaven, and urges the bachurim to be ehrliche Yidden, to daven and learn.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that a person is where his thoughts are, and that a Yid who wants to give Hashem nachas will seek purity in his tefillah and service even where it is not strictly required.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Shlomo HaMelech's tefillah that exiled Jews should turn toward Eretz Yisrael and the Beis Hamikdash, and explains how one in Boro Park should face, and above all have in mind that he stands in the Beis Hamikdash. He grounds this in the Ba'al Shem Tov's teaching that a person is where his thought is, which the Satmar Rav supported from the Gemara about a traveler who fixes his Shabbos place by a tree. He then turns to Ezra's takanah requiring immersion before davening, which was not accepted, and, through his rebbe's teaching from Mesillas Yesharim, contrasts Bilaam, who pressed Hashem to do his will, with Avraham Avinu, who went joyfully to the Akeidah. Hashem favors taharah, as seen in the Kohanim, the Rambam's own practice, the Kohen Gadol's immersions and immersion before Shabbos. A story of Rabbi Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld, Rabbeinu Tam tefillin and the shofar sounds illustrate doing more than the minimum.

en: When davening one should face Eretz Yisrael and, above all, have in mind that one is standing in the Beis Hamikdash, and this is accepted as if one were there.
Following the Ba'al Shem Tov, the Mashgiach teaches that a person is where his thought is: thinking of Torah places him in Gan Eden, and improper thoughts place him in Gehinnom.
Like a devoted child, a Yid should seek to do what gives Hashem pleasure even when he is not commanded, unlike Bilaam who tried to bend Hashem to his own will.
Although Ezra's takanah to immerse before davening was not upheld, Hashem favors service done in taharah, so immersion remains a midas chassidus.
A mikvah adds kedushah even to one who is not tamei, as seen from the Kohen Gadol's immersions on Yom Kippur and immersion before Shabbos.
Many customs beyond the letter of the law, such as Rabbeinu Tam tefillin, are ways to give Hashem nachas ruach.

title.en: Facing the Beis Hamikdash in tefillah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Shlomo HaMelech's tefillah that exiled Jews should turn toward the Beis Hamikdash, and explains that in Boro Park facing east is not exact, so one should turn halfway to the south. Above all, one should have in mind that he stands in the Beis Hamikdash, and it is accepted as if he were there.

title.en: A person is where his thought is

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Ba'al Shem Tov's teaching that a person is where his thought is, and the Satmar Rav's support from the Gemara about a traveler on Erev Shabbos who fixes his place by a tree near the city. Since one who has the Beis Hamikdash in mind is truly there, he should present himself accordingly.

title.en: Ezra's takanah and doing Hashem's will

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of Ezra's takanah that one who is tamei from keri must immerse before davening and learning, which was not accepted and was annulled, and notes that some Rishonim keep it for davening. He then recalls his rebbe's teaching, from Mesillas Yesharim, that a devoted servant or child does what the master or parent would like even without being told.

title.en: Bilaam versus Avraham at the Akeidah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings his rebbe's comparison between Bilaam, who claimed to follow Hashem's word yet tried three times to change His mind, and Avraham Avinu, who went with simcha to the Akeidah without one word of protest though it seemed to undo Hashem's promise. Rashi's reading of their walking together shows that both went with joy.

title.en: Hashem favors taharah

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that Hashem favors service in purity, from the Kohanim who may not serve when tamei, and concludes that immersion before davening is a midas chassidus. He brings the Rambam's letter that he himself always kept Ezra's takanah though he could not codify a chumrah as halachah, and adds the Kohen Gadol's five immersions, immersion before Shabbos, and the Arizal's immersion on Shabbos morning.

title.en: Rabbi Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld and the mikvah

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how someone asked Rabbi Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld whether going to the mikvah was not bittul Torah, and he answered that if a mikvah can make a goy into a Yid, it can make a Yid into a better Yid. The Mashgiach stresses he is not telling anyone to go daily, only that a Yid should want to give Hashem nachas ruach like a child who brings his mother a gift unasked.

title.en: Rabbeinu Tam tefillin, shofar and purity

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the custom to put on Rabbeinu Tam tefillin after marriage as an extra nachas ruach: both ways of ordering the parshiyos were old practice, the psak followed Rashi, yet the Zohar says both are needed, and after marriage one can be in greater purity. He compares the doubt over shevarim and teruah in shofar, and closes that purity of the body leads to purity of the soul.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach warns bachurim that leitzanus, the mocking spirit of the generation before Moshiach, uproots emunah, and through the last chapter of Malachi shows that in such a time those who fear Hashem must gather to strengthen one another.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Gemara's signs of ikvesa diMeshicha, the heels of Moshiach, and the chutzpah of the time. To receive from a rebbe, he says, one must stand beneath him with derech eretz, as Reb Baruch of Mezhbizh taught with the cup and the bottle. Jokes about rebbeim and teachers destroy this, and can even cost a teacher his parnassah. Leitzanus is the opposite of emunah: Pharaoh withstood the plagues only by mocking, and a single joke in a class of Reb Shraga Feivel Mendlowitz wiped out the seriousness of his talk. Emunah grows through tefillah said word by word, each word a diamond. Malachi, the last prophet, spoke to every generation until Eliyahu comes; he foresees Jews saying that serving Hashem does not pay, and promises that those who fear Hashem and gather to strengthen each other are written in a book of remembrance.

en: To receive from a rebbe one must be humble and stand beneath him, like a cup that must be lower than the bottle.
Joking about a rebbe or a teacher makes it impossible to receive from him in holiness and brings in bad middos.
Leitzanus is the opposite of emunah and uproots it, so a letz can have neither emunah nor yiras Shamayim.
Tefillah is emunah: one davens because one believes Hashem can help, and each word should be weighed like a diamond.
Malachi, as the last prophet, addressed all generations until Eliyahu Hanavi, and his last chapter speaks to the time before Moshiach.
When many say serving Hashem does not pay, those who fear Hashem gather and strengthen each other, and this is written in Hashem's book of remembrance.

title.en: Receiving from a rebbe in the time of chutzpah

summary.en: The Mashgiach recalls the Gemara's signs of ikvesa diMeshicha and the chutzpah of today, and brings Reb Baruch of Mezhbizh's mashal that a cup must be below the bottle to receive. He decries joking about rebbeim and teachers, notes that a teacher's parnassah is at stake, and tells how Reb Yaakov Kamenetsky rebuked a bachur who learned Mishnah Berurah during his English class.

title.en: Leitzanus uproots emunah: Pharaoh the letz

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that holiness is emunah and its opposite is leitzanus, and asks where the Torah shows Pharaoh joking. He tells of a boy's quip in Reb Shraga Feivel Mendlowitz's class, and answers that only mockery let Pharaoh stand up to plague after plague, since leitzanus dismisses even what one understands.

title.en: Tefillah as emunah, every word a diamond

summary.en: The Mashgiach praises the bachurim's crying out in davening and explains that tefillah means emunah, a cry for help to the One who can help, not a mouth exercise. Like dollar bills or diamonds, each word must be counted slowly; he brings the pasuk that Torah is sweeter than honey, and ties this to preparing for Shavuos.

title.en: Malachi, the last prophet, speaks to all generations

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that because Malachi was the last prophet, his words were meant for every generation until Eliyahu, like a message to people setting out on a long sea voyage. He reads the closing pesukim about sending Eliyahu Hanavi and the opening of the chapter about the messenger who clears the way.

title.en: Eliyahu's sudden coming and 'it does not pay'

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings a tradition from the Ba'al Shem Tov that Jews in a grocery store will suddenly hear that Eliyahu has come and run to shul. He continues through Malachi: who can endure the day of his coming, and the complaint of Jews that serving Hashem does not pay while the wicked enjoy life.

title.en: Those who fear Hashem gather together

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the time when people praise the wicked and their success, and explains the pasuk that then those who fear Hashem speak to one another. He applies it: Jews gathering for a mussar shmuess or a Shabbos meal with zemiros give Hashem great nachas, and it is written in His book of remembrance.

title.en: The day of judgment and 'remember the Torah of Moshe'

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the rest of the chapter: Hashem will have mercy on those who serve Him as a father on his son, the day will burn the wicked, and for those who fear Him a sun of righteousness will heal. He concludes that Malachi's last words, 'remember the Torah of Moshe' given at Chorev, must sustain Jews through the whole exile, even in dry times.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Shavuos is a living Kabbalas haTorah each year, demanding the greatest preparation, and that its whole purpose is reached in the davening and the reading of the Ten Commandments on Shavuos morning.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by noting that no yom tov has a preparation like Shavuos: the seven weeks of sefirah and the three days of hagbalah, together with teshuvah. A Jewish yom tov is not a commemoration like the Fourth of July; the same lights of Matan Torah come down each year. He tells how the Shinover Rav saw the thunder and lightning of Sinai in Belz, and how the Kotzker answered that believing is greater than seeing. Shavuos is a Rosh Hashanah on which each Jew's portion in Torah is decided, so one must make oneself a clean vessel, as the Blazhever Rav's heart showed. The night of learning is only the preparation; like a chasan who pays for everything but buys no ring, one who sleeps through davening misses the essence. Through the stories of the Imrei Emes and Reb Yisroel of Vizhnitz, emunah, the Torah lishmah of hearing krias haTorah, and Hashem's gift of love, he closes with blessings.

en: No yom tov has a preparation like Shavuos: the seven weeks of sefirah, the three days of hagbalah, and teshuvah.
A Jewish yom tov is not a commemoration; the same lights of Matan Torah come down again each year and Hashem gives the Torah anew.
Shavuos is a Rosh Hashanah on which each Jew's portion in Torah for the year is decided.
Besides Hashem giving the Torah, a Jew must receive it, and for that he must make himself a clean vessel.
Staying up on Shavuos night is only a preparation; the essence is the davening and the Torah reading in the morning, and one who cannot do both should sleep.
Listening to krias haTorah, especially the Ten Commandments, is a way to receive emunah and to learn Torah lishmah.

title.en: The unique preparation for Shavuos

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Shavuos has a preparation unlike any yom tov: sefirah, teshuvah and the three days of hagbalah. He contrasts a Jewish yom tov with the Fourth of July: it is not a commemoration, since the same lights of Matan Torah come down every year.

title.en: Hearing the thunder of Sinai

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how the Shinover Rav saw the thunder and lightning of Sinai during the reading of the Ten Commandments in Belz and later in Sanz, and how the Kotzker answered that his belief is greater than another's seeing. He adds that on Shavuos one is judged on how much Torah and devotion he will have, more than on Rosh Hashanah's bread and milk.

title.en: Shavuos as Rosh Hashanah; a clean vessel

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that Shavuos is a Rosh Hashanah, when each Jew's portion in Torah is decided. Hashem gives the Torah, but the Jew must receive it; like costly wine that no one pours into a dirty cup, he must purify himself. He tells of the Blazhever Rav, whose heart beat irregularly before Shavuos because he had to receive the Torah.

title.en: Shavuos night and the holiness of the day

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the success of the year, and perhaps of life, depends on Shavuos. Citing the Ohr HaChaim, he explains that on Shavuos night a purity descends because sefirah is complete, which is why one learns all night, so as to daven properly and hear the Torah reading. He describes the custom of great tzaddikim not to speak until after Mussaf, cautioning that each must act by his level.

title.en: The chasan who forgot the ring

summary.en: The Mashgiach gives a mashal of a chasan who pays for the musicians, photographer and flowers but has no ring, so there is no kiddushin. So too one who counts sefirah and stays up all night but sleeps through the davening and the Ten Commandments: the night is only the music, the essence is the chuppah. He says one must beg Hashem in Ahavah Rabbah, and whoever cannot stay up and still daven properly should go to sleep.

title.en: Ahavah Rabbah, the Imrei Emes and Vizhnitz

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes how chassidim once spent an hour on Ahavah Rabbah of Shavuos. He tells of the Imrei Emes, who instituted early davening and told his chassidim to sleep on Shavuos night so as to daven with fervor, and of Reb Yisroel of Vizhnitz, who told bachurim rushing to daven in order to sleep that one sleeps in order to daven, not the reverse.

title.en: Emunah, Torah lishmah and the gift of love

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Rambam counts emunah, from Anochi, as the first mitzvah, and that on Shavuos one receives it by listening to the Torah reading, which is itself Torah lishmah. He links Shavuos to the completion of sefirah and to Moshiach, gives a mashal of a lover's best gift, and closes with blessings to receive the Torah with love, awe and joy.

oneLiner.en: Facing the low days of Tamuz and Av and the trials of emunah before Moshiach, the Mashgiach tells bachurim to ignore doubts rather than argue with them, and to truly wait and hope for Moshiach every day.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens after Shavuos: the coming days of Sivan, Tamuz and Av are days of mourning, yet with Moshiach they will become the greatest yomim tovim, as the prophet Zechariah says. Until then one prepares with teshuvah, Torah, tefillah and guarding the eyes, since today's trials are unprecedented. The impurity of the street brings doubts in emunah; quoting the Or HaChaim, he says that before Moshiach Jews will fall even into the fiftieth gate, and only the power of Torah holds them. Such doubts are like a 'bug' in the head, comparable to OCD, and the advice is to ignore them and not answer, as the Vilna Gaon advised a man who saw a cross while davening. Emunah before Moshiach is like climbing a smooth wall, but Hashem is with a Jew. He describes the wars and dangers of the time, including Iran as Paras of the Midrash, and stresses the mitzvah to hope for Moshiach, who can come any day.

en: The fast days and the Three Weeks are destined to become the greatest yomim tovim when Moshiach comes, and the present days call for teshuvah together with hope.
Doubts in emunah that come from the impurity of the street are not real questions but a 'bug' in the head; the advice is to ignore them and not to answer them.
Before Moshiach, holding on to emunah is as hard as climbing a smooth wall, yet Hashem is with a Jew even in the worst situation.
It is a mitzvah to wait and hope for Moshiach; one who says 'ki lishuascha kivinu' without waiting is saying an untruth before Hashem.
Moshiach can come on any day, even before the expected time, and this year after shemittah is especially auspicious.
Every Jew carries a spark of Moshiach's soul, and each must rectify his own part.

title.en: Days of mourning that will turn to yom tov

summary.en: After Shavuos the Mashgiach looks ahead to the fast for the massacres of Tach v'Tat in Sivan and to the Three Weeks. He says that when Moshiach comes these will be the happiest weeks of the year, describes a tzaddik who held a cup on Tisha B'Av to show how kiddush will be made then, and brings Zechariah's prophecy that the fasts will become days of joy.

title.en: Preparing for the low days amid great trials

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that the week after Shavuos still belongs to the yom tov, then turns to the preparation for the coming low days: learning, davening, good middos and above all guarding the eyes and thoughts. The world's impurity is unprecedented, and it leads to doubts in emunah.

title.en: Doubts in emunah: ignore, don't answer

summary.en: Bringing the Or HaChaim that before Moshiach Jews will fall into the fiftieth gate of impurity, the Mashgiach explains why doubts are so common today. He calls them a 'bug' in the head, compares them to OCD, tells the story of the Vilna Gaon's advice to a man who saw a cross while davening, and concludes that one must ignore such thoughts and never debate them.

title.en: Emunah before Moshiach: climbing a smooth wall

summary.en: The Mashgiach cites tzaddikim that before Moshiach emunah will be as hard as climbing a smooth wall, and Rebbe Nachman of Breslov that a Jew with simple faith then will be as great a wonder as the Ba'al Shem Tov. The Satan fights with his last strength because he knows his end is near; one must pray for clear emunah and say the Ani Maamins.

title.en: Chevlei Moshiach and the Midrash about Paras

summary.en: The Mashgiach speaks of the wars and troubles before Moshiach, the danger to Jews in Eretz Yisroel and everywhere, and Iran's wish for a bomb. He brings the Midrash that Paras will threaten to destroy the world and Hashem will tell the Jews not to fear, for the time of their redemption has come, and identifies Paras with Iran; one must prepare with Torah and mitzvos to greet Moshiach without shame.

title.en: The mitzvah to wait for Moshiach

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that a person is asked whether he hoped for the salvation, and argues that saying 'ki lishuascha kivinu kol hayom' in davening or 'ki mechakim anachnu lach' in the Shabbos kedushah without truly waiting would be a lie before Hashem. The Chachamim instituted these words for ehrliche Yidden who really wait.

title.en: Moshiach hidden in Tamuz and Av; 'hinei Elokeinu zeh'

summary.en: The Mashgiach says Moshiach lies hidden in the months of Tamuz and Av, citing the Midrash that he is born on Tisha B'Av. Hashem asks through Tzefaniah that Jews wait for Him, and Yeshayahu's words 'hinei Elokeinu zeh kivinu lo' can be said only by one who truly hoped.

title.en: Remembering Yerushalayim; Moshiach can come any day

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Dovid HaMelech's oath 'im eshkacheich Yerushalayim', from which comes the custom of breaking a glass at the chuppah, and says one must constantly remember and pray for Yerushalayim. Moshiach is not tied to any time and can come any moment, even before the next Maariv.

title.en: Before its time; the spark of Moshiach in every Jew

summary.en: From the exile in Mitzrayim, foretold as four hundred years but ended after two hundred and ten, the Mashgiach shows that redemption can come early. He points to the wars of the time and the Gemara that Moshiach comes in the year after shemittah, says every Jew has a spark of Moshiach's soul to rectify, and closes that sad days can be turned into days of joy.

catalogTitle: Our Steadfast Faith in Hashem's Salvation ('פירוש על פרק כ “יענך ה' ביום צרה”)

oneLiner.en: Learning Tehillim chapter 20, Lamenatzeach … Ya'ancha Hashem b'yom tzarah, the Mashgiach explains that in a time of danger before Moshiach a Jew sings and thanks Hashem even before the salvation, because he is certain it will come.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by explaining why he will speak in English, then begins a series on the chapters of Tehillim said in davening, starting with chapter 20 because Klal Yisrael is in an eis tzarah. He recalls how Hashem saved the Jews when Rommel stood at the gates of Eretz Yisrael and in the Six Day War, and brings the Zohar that Yaakov Avinu saved three of his four brachos for the troubles before Moshiach. The troubles before Moshiach are birth pangs; Chazal say a woman in labor sighs seventy times, and the chapter's seventy words match them, its last word, kareinu, being our time. Dovid sings to the One who grants victory and thanks Him before the yeshua. Through the verses he explains Elokei Yaakov, the minchah of a poor man, the request that Hashem's Name be whole, the lessons of history, and that Jews rise after they fall.

en: The Mashgiach says Klal Yisrael is in an eis tzarah and needs great mercy, so he begins with the chapter of Tehillim that is the tefillah for a time of trouble.
The troubles before Moshiach are birth pangs, and the seventy words of the chapter correspond to the seventy sighs of a woman in labor; we are now at its last word, kareinu.
Dovid does not cry in his trouble but sings to the One who grants victory, and thanks Hashem already before the salvation, because he is sure it will come.

Hashem is called the G-d of Yaakov because Yaakov's life was a continuous chain of troubles which he bore with bitachon, and his journeys represent the Jewish people's journey through galus to the geulah.
Hashem does not expect from this generation the avodah of earlier tzaddikim; He regards our small offering like a rich korban.
From history and their own experience Jews know that at moments of seeming despair Hashem helps, and unlike nations who trust in chariots and horses, they rise again after they fall.
